body.heading: Every sequence is equally surprising
paragraphs: Flip a coin four times. The chance of heads, heads, heads, heads is 1 in 16. But here is the twist: the chance of heads, tails, tails, heads is also exactly 1 in 16. Every specific sequence of four flips has the same probability. HHHH only looks special because it is the one your eye picks out.

So when a streak happens, nothing has gone wrong. The coin has not become biased and it does not owe you a tails. Each flip is fresh, and the streak is just one of the many patterns that were all equally unlikely before you started.

body.heading: Why streaks are almost guaranteed
paragraphs: In a run of 20 flips, there are 17 overlapping windows of four flips, and each window has some chance of being all heads or all tails. Add those chances together and a streak of four somewhere in the run becomes more likely than not. In 100 flips, the longest run of heads is typically around six or seven.

This is why 'hot streaks' in sport and games need careful handling. Some streaks really do come from skill, but many are exactly what pure chance produces. The maths does not say streaks are meaningless - it says you should expect them even when nothing special is going on.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Flip a coin 50 times, write down every result in order, and find your longest streak. Compare with a friend. One of you probably produced a run of four or five, and neither coin was cheating.

For a sharper test, ask a friend to invent a fake sequence of 20 flips without flipping anything. People inventing results almost always alternate too much and avoid long streaks, so their fake looks tidy - and that tidiness is exactly what gives them away.

takeaway: A fair coin makes streaks because every exact sequence is equally unlikely - patterns that catch your eye are not the same as patterns that break the rules.
